summary: Provides the test plan and results used to advance RFC 2680, which defines one-way packet loss metrics, along the Standards Track. Two independent implementations were tested against its key requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: Before calling a ruler official, you check it with two different measurers. This is the report of such a check for a packet-loss measure.

questions: one-way packet loss metric implementation report
how to test a packet loss metric
what is the anderson darling k sample test
subtitle: The test plan and results showing that two independent tools read the one-way packet loss metric the same way.

tldr.problem: RFC 2680 defines one-way packet loss metrics, and to advance it on the Standards Track the IETF needed evidence that its definitions are clear and unambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: Two completely independent implementations, NetProbe and Perfas+, measured loss across a tunnelled test path with a network emulator, and their results were compared with statistical tests (Anderson-Darling) against limits set in advance.
tldr.outcome: The results were equivalent, so the memo concludes RFC 2680 should be advanced, with a few small text edits. The revision itself was left for future action.

today: RFC 7290 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the evidence supporting the advancement of RFC 2680, and it says the revision of RFC 2680 itself was left for future action.

sections.title: Why Test a Metric Definition
sections.content:
The IETF IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group wanted to advance its metrics along the Standards Track. Following the consensus captured in RFC 6576, equivalent results from independent implementations are sufficient evidence that a metric specification is clear and unambiguous. It is the metric-specification version of protocol interoperability.

So the thing under test is the definition in the RFC text, not the tools. The process either gives confidence that the wording is clear or shows where it should be revised. Comparing the specific implementations is explicitly a non-goal. The memo follows the report template in RFC 6808.

The plan covers the critical requirements of RFC 2680. The memo notes there are only five relevant uses of the word MUST in RFC 2680 outside boilerplate, plus at least one implied requirement in its Section 3.6.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people read the same recipe and bake the same cake, the recipe is probably clear. This memo checks whether two measuring tools read the packet-loss recipe the same way.

sections.title: The Test Setup
sections.content:
Two implementations were used. NetProbe (version 5.8.5) sends UDP packets of variable size with Periodic or Poisson sample distributions. Perfas+ (version 3.1, from Deutsche Telekom) uses UDP unicast packets and can use Periodic, Poisson or uniform streams.

Test traffic crossed the Internet inside an L2TPv3 tunnel. The tunnel headers hide the test equipment's addresses and ports from hash functions that would spread streams across parallel paths. VLANs at each end were looped back, so each stream crosses the tunnel twice but looks one-way to the test equipment. A host running the Linux netem network emulator added delay, loss and reordering.

Streams were at least 300 packets, at 1 or 10 packets per second, with IP packet sizes of 64, 340 and 500 bytes. The packet Type-P was IP-UDP with Best Effort DSCP. The memo admits the links to the emulator turned out to be 100 Mbps half duplex, which probably added a little delay variation.
sections.plainLanguage: The testers built a racetrack with a tunnel and a gadget that drops and delays toy cars on purpose, then sent cars past two different counters to see if both counted the same.

sections.title: Equivalence Limits Set in Advance
sections.content:
The working group agreed that the threshold for calling results equivalent should be known before cross-implementation comparisons. The allowed error only needs to be big enough to catch a real misinterpretation of the specification and to cover path differences that could not be avoided in the VLAN-loopback setup.

For Anderson-Darling K-sample (ADK) comparisons, the required confidence factor is the smallest of 0.95 at 1-packet resolution, or the smallest confidence factor of the two same-implementation comparisons under the same conditions. For Anderson-Darling Goodness-of-Fit comparisons, the required significance level is 0.05, or 5%, as in RFC 2330.

The memo also checks that load does not cause false loss. The maximum load between two NetProbe instances was 11.5 Mbit/s split equally among three unicast streams, and steady resource usage was judged not to add error.
sections.plainLanguage: They decided how close two scores must be before calling them the same, and wrote that down before looking at any scores.

sections.title: The Tests and Their Results
sections.content:
ADK loss comparison (6.1). Loss counts from the two tools were compared for 340-byte Periodic, 64-byte Periodic and 64-byte Poisson streams, each with a 10% emulated loss ratio. All three passed the criterion t.obs < 1.960. The 64-byte Poisson case passed only barely (1.93129 when adjusted for ties). The memo concludes the tools produce equivalent one-way loss measurements.

Delay threshold (6.2). RFC 2680 says a packet arriving after a maximum waiting time is lost. With a 3 second threshold and the emulator adding 3 seconds of constant delay, NetProbe declared 342 packets lost. Perfas+ has a fixed threshold of about one minute, but applying a post-processing step gave 195 lost. The memo takes the position that post-processing is compliant and RFC 2680 should say so.

Reordering (6.3). The emulator used 2000 ms delay with 1000 ms variation to reorder packets. Despite extensive reordering, the loss counts still passed the ADK criterion.

Poisson sending (6.4). Both tools were configured for lambda = 1 packet per second. The goodness-of-fit criterion from RFC 2330 requires AD <= 2.492 at 5% significance, and all tested sets of packets passed.

Statistics (6.5). Both tools implement the average loss statistic, which they call the loss ratio.
sections.plainLanguage: They tested four things: do both counters agree on lost cars, do both treat very late cars as lost, do they cope with cars arriving out of order, and do they send cars at truly random times. The answer each time was yes.

sections.title: Conclusions for Revising RFC 2680
sections.content:
The memo concludes that RFC 2680 should be advanced on the Standards Track, with edits that are not significant enough to affect maturity:

  • Rename Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Ave to Type-P-One-way-Delay-Packet-Loss-Ratio.
  • State that implementing the loss delay threshold by post-processing is compliant.
  • Reference the guidance on reporting metrics in RFC 6703.

There are at least two errata for RFC 2680 that should be folded in, and revising authors should review all errata filed at the time. The revised text was ready for review but waited on work to update the IPPM Framework (RFC 2330), so approval of the revision was left for future action.
sections.plainLanguage: The check passed, so the packet-loss measure can become official after a few small wording fixes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo adds nothing new on security. It says the considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant here too, and points to RFC 4656 and RFC 5357.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring a real network can disturb it, so the usual care for network measuring applies.
